title: Red Winemaking in Burgundy
description: The decisions that shape Burgundy's Pinot Noir — from whole-cluster fermentation to oak aging and élevage.
lessons.0.title: Whole Cluster vs Destemmed: The Defining Choice
lessons.0.slides.0.title: Whole Cluster vs Destemmed: The Defining Choice
lessons.0.slides.0.subtitle: 15 minutes
lessons.0.slides.0.description: The single most discussed winemaking decision in Burgundy — whether to include stems in fermentation — and how it shapes the wine's architecture.
lessons.0.slides.1.title: What Is Whole-Cluster Fermentation?
lessons.0.slides.1.content: Whole-cluster fermentation means placing entire, intact grape bunches — stems and all — into the fermentation vessel, rather than destemming (removing stems) first. The choice affects tannin structure, aromatic character, colour and aging potential profoundly.
lessons.0.slides.1.keyPoints.0: Whole cluster (grappes entières): entire bunches enter the vat; stems contribute tannin, spice and structure
lessons.0.slides.1.keyPoints.1: Destemmed (égrappé): grapes separated from stems before fermentation; cleaner, more immediate fruit expression
lessons.0.slides.1.keyPoints.2: Partial whole cluster: many estates use a blend — e.g. 30% whole cluster + 70% destemmed
lessons.0.slides.1.keyPoints.3: The percentage varies by producer, vintage and parcel — there is no single correct answer
lessons.0.slides.2.title: Arguments for Whole-Cluster Fermentation
lessons.0.slides.2.content: The case for keeping stems: when fully ripe and lignified, stems contribute positive aromatic and structural elements that add complexity and longevity.
lessons.0.slides.2.keyPoints.0: Fresh aromatic lift: ripe stems contribute spice, forest floor and floral nuances
lessons.0.slides.2.keyPoints.1: Lower alcohol: stems absorb alcohol, resulting in a fractionally lighter wine
lessons.0.slides.2.keyPoints.2: Natural drainage channels: stems create air pockets in the cap, facilitating CO₂ release
lessons.0.slides.2.keyPoints.3: Structural elegance: whole-cluster wines often show finer, more integrated tannin with age
lessons.0.slides.2.keyPoints.4: Proponents: Henri Jayer (pioneer of destemming) reversed trend — many younger producers returning to whole cluster
lessons.0.slides.3.title: Arguments for Destemming
lessons.0.slides.3.content: The case for removing stems: Henri Jayer, the legendary 20th-century Vosne-Romanée producer, championed 100% destemming and transformed Burgundy's winemaking philosophy.
lessons.0.slides.3.keyPoints.0: Cleaner fruit: removing unripe stems eliminates vegetal, herbaceous flavours
lessons.0.slides.3.keyPoints.1: Earlier approachability: destemmed wines open up faster, with less harsh tannin in youth
lessons.0.slides.3.keyPoints.2: Better in challenging vintages: when stems are not fully ripe, destemming is essential
lessons.0.slides.3.keyPoints.3: Consistent style: easier to replicate across vintages
lessons.0.slides.4.title: Notable Producers and Their Philosophy
lessons.0.slides.4.points.0: 🍷 Henri Jayer — championed 100% destemming, transformed Burgundy winemaking in the 1970s–90s
lessons.0.slides.4.points.1: 🍷 Domaine Leroy — varies by vintage; high percentage whole cluster for structure
lessons.0.slides.4.points.2: 🍷 Domaine de la Romanée-Conti — increasing use of whole cluster in recent vintages
lessons.0.slides.4.points.3: 🍷 Domaine Armand Rousseau — predominantly destemmed, Jayer-influenced clean style
lessons.0.slides.4.points.4: 🍷 Domaine Dujac — famous for high percentage whole cluster; spice and wild aromatics
lessons.0.slides.5.title: 🧠 Knowledge Check
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.0.question: What is whole-cluster fermentation?
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.0.options.0: A. Fermenting with the grape seeds still inside the berries
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.0.options.1: B. Placing entire intact bunches — stems and all — into the fermentation vessel
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.0.options.2: C. Fermentation in large barrels rather than open vats
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.0.options.3: D. A technique exclusive to Chardonnay white wine production
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.0.explanati: Whole-cluster fermentation means intact bunches — including stems — are placed in the fermentation vessel. The stems contribute tannin, spice and structure, and create natural drainage channels in the fermenting cap.
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.1.question: Which legendary winemaker championed 100% destemming and transformed Burgundy's winemaking?
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.1.explanati: Henri Jayer (1922–2006) of Vosne-Romanée was the most influential Burgundy winemaker of the 20th century. He championed 100% destemming for clean, pure fruit expression, and his philosophy dominated Burgundy winemaking from the 1970s through the 1990s.
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.2.question: What is a typical argument FOR using whole clusters?
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.2.options.0: A. Whole clusters eliminate the need for sorting
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.2.options.1: B. Ripe stems add spice, freshness and finer tannin structure with age
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.2.options.2: C. Whole clusters always produce higher alcohol
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.2.explanati: When stems are fully ripe and lignified (woody), they contribute positive aromatic complexity — spice, forest floor, floral notes — and create structural elegance. Whole-cluster wines also tend to have slightly lower alcohol because stems absorb alcohol during fermentation.
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.3.question: In a vintage with partially unripe stems, what is the correct approach?
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.3.options.0: A. Always use 100% whole cluster to maximise structure
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.3.options.1: B. Destem to avoid green, vegetal flavours from unripe stems contaminating the wine
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.3.options.2: C. Add stems from older vintages
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.3.options.3: D. Reduce fermentation temperature to mask stem flavours
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.3.explanati: Unripe stems taste bitter and vegetal — they add negative flavour compounds to the wine. In cooler, less ripe vintages, destemming (removing stems) is essential to avoid these off-flavours. Many producers use a higher whole-cluster percentage only in warm, ripe years when stems are fully lignified.
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.4.question: Which estate is famous for a high percentage of whole-cluster fermentation and distinctive spice character?
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.4.options.2: C. Domaine Gros Frère et Sœur
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.4.options.3: D. Domaine Comte Georges de Vogüé
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.4.explanati: Domaine Dujac (Jacques and Jeremy Seysses, Morey-Saint-Denis) is celebrated for its high whole-cluster percentage — typically 50–100% depending on the year. Their wines show a distinctive wild spice, forest floor and florality that is directly attributable to this style.
lessons.0.slides.6.title: Summary
lessons.0.slides.6.content: The whole-cluster debate has defined Burgundy winemaking discussions for three decades. Whether to destem, partially destem or keep everything is one of the most personal and consequential choices a Burgundy winemaker makes — and the results are directly tasted in the glass.
lessons.1.title: Cold Soak, Fermentation and Extraction
lessons.1.slides.0.title: Cold Soak, Fermentation and Extraction
lessons.1.slides.0.subtitle: 15 minutes
lessons.1.slides.0.description: How pre-fermentation cold soak extracts colour and aroma without tannin, and how fermentation decisions shape Burgundy's character.
lessons.1.slides.1.title: 🧊 Pre-Fermentation Cold Soak
lessons.1.slides.1.content: Cold soak (macération préfermentaire à froid) holds the must at low temperature (5–10°C) for 3–7 days before fermentation begins. Cold inhibits yeast activity while allowing water-soluble compounds to extract.
lessons.1.slides.1.keyPoints.0: Extracts colour (anthocyanins) and aromatic compounds without extracting harsh tannins
lessons.1.slides.1.keyPoints.1: Temperature: 5–10°C prevents yeast activity; SO₂ or dry ice used to suppress wild yeast
lessons.1.slides.1.keyPoints.3: Result: deeper colour, more aromatic intensity in the final wine
lessons.1.slides.1.keyPoints.4: Debate: some producers avoid it, fearing pre-fermentation oxidation
lessons.1.slides.2.title: 🍾 Indigenous vs Cultivated Yeasts
lessons.1.slides.2.content: Burgundy's most philosophically committed producers ferment with indigenous (natural) yeasts that live on grape skins and in the cellar — arguing this adds terroir character. Others use selected commercial yeasts for predictability.
lessons.1.slides.2.keyPoints.0: Indigenous yeasts (levures indigènes): unpredictable, slow fermentation; claimed to add complexity and terroir expression
lessons.1.slides.2.keyPoints.1: Commercial yeasts (levures sélectionnées): reliable, fast fermentation; predictable aromatic profile
lessons.1.slides.2.keyPoints.2: Risk of indigenous yeasts: stuck fermentation; production of off-flavours by undesirable yeast strains
lessons.1.slides.2.keyPoints.3: Top estates (DRC, Leroy, Rousseau) all use indigenous yeasts
lessons.1.slides.3.title: 🛢️ Fermentation Vessels
lessons.1.slides.3.content: The choice of fermentation vessel shapes the wine's oxidative exposure, thermal mass, temperature profile and ultimately its structure and texture.
lessons.1.slides.3.keyPoints.0: Open wooden vats (cuves ouvertes en bois): traditional; gentle heat retention; allows easy pigeage (punching down)
lessons.1.slides.3.keyPoints.1: Stainless steel tanks: precise temperature control; neutral flavour; hygienic
lessons.1.slides.3.keyPoints.2: Concrete tanks: natural insulation; no flavour contribution; increasingly fashionable
lessons.1.slides.3.keyPoints.3: Fermentation temperature: 28–32°C typical for Pinot Noir (higher than Bordeaux) to extract colour and aroma
lessons.1.slides.4.title: 💡 Key Take-aways
lessons.1.slides.4.points.0: 🍷 Cold soak extracts colour and aroma without harsh tannin — a quality tool used by most top estates
lessons.1.slides.4.points.1: 🍷 Indigenous yeasts are the hallmark of artisan Burgundy production
lessons.1.slides.4.points.2: 🍷 Open wooden vats are traditional Burgundy; each vessel type delivers different textural results
lessons.1.slides.4.points.3: 🍷 Fermentation temperature is higher for Pinot Noir than for Cabernet — colour and fragrance demand it
lessons.1.slides.5.title: 🧠 Knowledge Check
lessons.1.slides.5.questions.0.question: What is the primary purpose of pre-fermentation cold soak?
lessons.1.slides.5.questions.0.options.0: A. To kill harmful bacteria in the must
lessons.1.slides.5.questions.0.options.1: B. To extract colour and aromatics from the skins before fermentation starts, without extracting harsh tannins
lessons.1.slides.5.questions.0.options.2: C. To concentrate sugar in the must through evaporation
lessons.1.slides.5.questions.0.options.3: D. To slow down malolactic fermentation
lessons.1.slides.5.questions.0.explanati: Cold soak works because at 5–10°C, water-soluble colour pigments (anthocyanins) and aromatic compounds leach from the skins into the must, while alcohol-soluble tannins remain largely locked in the grape skins. The result is better colour and aromatic depth without harsh tannin.
lessons.1.slides.5.questions.1.question: What is the main risk of using indigenous yeasts?
lessons.1.slides.5.questions.1.options.0: A. They produce wines with too much tannin
lessons.1.slides.5.questions.1.options.1: B. They are more expensive than commercial yeasts
lessons.1.slides.5.questions.1.options.2: C. Stuck fermentation or production of off-flavours by unwanted yeast strains
lessons.1.slides.5.questions.1.options.3: D. They cannot survive in cold cellars
lessons.1.slides.5.questions.1.explanati: Indigenous (natural) yeasts are unpredictable — fermentation may start slowly, stop partway through (stuck fermentation), or produce unwanted aromatic compounds if undesirable yeast strains dominate. Top estates accept this risk because they believe natural yeasts add terroir character and complexity.
lessons.1.slides.5.questions.2.question: Why do top Burgundy estates prefer open wooden vats for fermentation?
lessons.1.slides.5.questions.2.options.0: A. Wood adds oak flavour to the wine during fermentation
lessons.1.slides.5.questions.2.options.1: B. They are cheaper than stainless steel
lessons.1.slides.5.questions.2.options.2: C. They allow easy punching down (pigeage) and gentle heat retention without adding flavour
lessons.1.slides.5.questions.2.options.3: D. Stainless steel tanks are not permitted under Burgundy AOC rules
lessons.1.slides.5.questions.2.explanati: Open wooden vats are traditional in Burgundy because they facilitate easy manual punching down (pigeage), allow gentle heat retention, and their non-reactive wood surface imparts no oak flavour — it is the barrel aging afterwards that provides that element.
lessons.1.slides.5.questions.3.question: At what approximate temperature is Pinot Noir typically fermented in Burgundy?
lessons.1.slides.5.questions.3.options.2: C. 28–32°C (warm; to extract colour and aroma)
lessons.1.slides.5.questions.3.options.3: D. 38–42°C (very warm; for maximum tannin extraction)
lessons.1.slides.5.questions.3.explanati: Pinot Noir is typically fermented at 28–32°C in Burgundy. This relatively warm temperature efficiently extracts anthocyanins (colour) and fragrant aromatic compounds from the thin Pinot Noir skins, which require heat to release their contents.
lessons.1.slides.5.questions.4.question: What distinguishes indigenous yeast fermentation from commercial yeast fermentation?
lessons.1.slides.5.questions.4.options.0: A. Indigenous yeasts produce sweeter wines with higher residual sugar
lessons.1.slides.5.questions.4.options.1: B. Indigenous yeasts are naturally present on grape skins and in the cellar; commercial yeasts are laboratory-selected strains
lessons.1.slides.5.questions.4.options.2: C. Commercial yeasts are the only option approved under AOC law
lessons.1.slides.5.questions.4.options.3: D. Indigenous yeasts work only at cold temperatures
lessons.1.slides.5.questions.4.explanati: Indigenous (native/wild) yeasts live naturally on grape skins and in the cellar environment, and activate spontaneously. Commercial yeasts are laboratory-selected strains added by the winemaker for predictable, reliable fermentation. Top Burgundy estates favour indigenous yeasts for their claimed contribution to complexity and place character.
lessons.1.slides.6.title: Summary
lessons.1.slides.6.content: Cold soak, indigenous yeast fermentation and thoughtful vessel choice are the building blocks of Burgundy's red winemaking approach — all aimed at extracting the maximum aromatic character and colour from the delicate, thin-skinned Pinot Noir grape.
lessons.2.title: Extraction: Pigeage, Remontage and the Press
lessons.2.slides.0.title: Extraction: Pigeage, Remontage and the Press
lessons.2.slides.0.subtitle: 12 minutes
lessons.2.slides.0.description: How Burgundy producers extract colour, tannin and flavour from the grape skins — and why gentleness is paramount for Pinot Noir.
lessons.2.slides.1.title: 🙌 Punching Down (Pigeage)
lessons.2.slides.1.content: During red wine fermentation, CO₂ pushes grape skins to the surface, forming a cap (chapeau). Pigeage (punching down) plunges this cap back into the liquid to extract colour, tannin and flavour compounds.
lessons.2.slides.1.keyPoints.0: Traditional method: a worker physically punches the cap down with a wooden or stainless tool
lessons.2.slides.1.keyPoints.1: Frequency: typically 2–3 times per day during peak fermentation
lessons.2.slides.1.keyPoints.2: For Pinot Noir: gentle pigeage preferred — Pinot's thin skins can be over-extracted, producing harsh tannins
lessons.2.slides.1.keyPoints.3: Alternative: remontage (pumping over) is less disruptive but provides slightly less skin contact
lessons.2.slides.2.title: 💧 Pumping Over (Remontage)
lessons.2.slides.2.content: Remontage pumps fermenting juice from the bottom of the tank and sprays it over the top of the cap. It provides gentler, more uniform extraction than pigeage.
lessons.2.slides.2.keyPoints.0: Method: juice drawn from the base of the vat is pumped to irrigate the cap from above
lessons.2.slides.2.keyPoints.1: Result: uniform colour and flavour extraction; promotes yeast activity; cools the cap
lessons.2.slides.2.keyPoints.2: Preferred in: larger operations or when very gentle extraction is desired
lessons.2.slides.2.keyPoints.3: Combined approach: many estates use both pigeage and remontage at different stages of fermentation
lessons.2.slides.3.title: 🍇 Pressing and Press Wine (Vin de Presse)
lessons.2.slides.3.content: After fermentation completes, free-run wine (vin de goutte) is drained off and the remaining skins are pressed. The press wine is richer in tannin and colour.
lessons.2.slides.3.keyPoints.0: Free-run wine (vin de goutte): the finest fraction; delicate and aromatic; first to be removed
lessons.2.slides.3.keyPoints.1: Press wine (vin de presse): more extracted, richer in tannin and colour; used to add structure
lessons.2.slides.3.keyPoints.2: Press fractions: different press pressures yield progressively harsher wine; only the best fractions are used
lessons.2.slides.3.keyPoints.3: Final blend: winemaker adds a percentage of press wine (typically 5–20%) to enhance structure and depth
lessons.2.slides.4.title: 💡 Key Take-aways
lessons.2.slides.4.points.0: 🍷 Pigeage (punching down) is Burgundy's traditional extraction method — but gentleness is critical for Pinot Noir
lessons.2.slides.4.points.1: 🍷 Remontage (pumping over) offers more uniform, gentler extraction
lessons.2.slides.4.points.2: 🍷 Press wine adds structure and depth — the best estates carefully select which fractions to use
lessons.2.slides.4.points.3: 🍷 Pinot Noir requires less extraction than Cabernet — over-extraction is a common winemaking error in Burgundy
lessons.2.slides.5.title: 🧠 Knowledge Check
lessons.2.slides.5.questions.0.question: What is pigeage in Burgundy red winemaking?
lessons.2.slides.5.questions.0.options.0: A. The process of blending different parcels after fermentation
lessons.2.slides.5.questions.0.options.1: B. Punching the cap of grape skins back down into the fermenting liquid to extract colour and flavour
lessons.2.slides.5.questions.0.options.2: C. Adding yeasts at the start of fermentation
lessons.2.slides.5.questions.0.options.3: D. The final pressing of grape skins after fermentation
lessons.2.slides.5.questions.0.explanati: Pigeage (punching down) physically submerges the cap of floating skins back into the fermenting liquid. This extracts colour pigments, flavour compounds and tannins from the skins. For Pinot Noir, gentle pigeage is preferred because the thin skins can yield harsh, bitter tannins if over-extracted.
lessons.2.slides.5.questions.1.question: What is remontage?
lessons.2.slides.5.questions.1.options.0: A. Transferring wine from barrel to barrel
lessons.2.slides.5.questions.1.options.1: B. Pumping fermenting juice from the base of the tank to spray over the cap
lessons.2.slides.5.questions.1.options.2: C. Removing dead yeast cells after fermentation
lessons.2.slides.5.questions.1.options.3: D. Topping up barrels to prevent oxidation
lessons.2.slides.5.questions.1.explanati: Remontage (pumping over) draws fermenting juice from the bottom of the vat and pumps it through a pipe to spray over the top of the skin cap. It provides uniform extraction and cools the cap, but is generally gentler than pigeage (punching down).
lessons.2.slides.5.questions.2.question: What is 'vin de presse' (press wine)?
lessons.2.slides.5.questions.2.options.0: A. Wine pressed from unripe grapes
lessons.2.slides.5.questions.2.options.1: B. The wine extracted by pressing the skins after fermentation, richer in tannin and colour than free-run wine
lessons.2.slides.5.questions.2.options.2: C. A second fermentation in the press
lessons.2.slides.5.questions.2.options.3: D. Wine made exclusively from pressed (rather than whole) grapes
lessons.2.slides.5.questions.2.explanati: Vin de presse (press wine) is extracted from the grape skins after free-run wine has drained off naturally. It is denser in colour, richer in tannin and more concentrated — winemakers add a calculated percentage (5–20%) to the free-run wine to add backbone and depth.
lessons.2.slides.5.questions.3.question: Why must extraction be gentler for Pinot Noir than for Cabernet Sauvignon?
lessons.2.slides.5.questions.3.options.0: A. Pinot Noir is harvested later, so it is over-ripe and needs less extraction
lessons.2.slides.5.questions.3.options.1: B. Pinot Noir has thin skins that yield harsh, bitter tannins if over-extracted
lessons.2.slides.5.questions.3.options.2: C. Cabernet Sauvignon is naturally lower in tannin and needs more extraction
lessons.2.slides.5.questions.3.options.3: D. Pinot Noir is fermented in larger vats where extraction happens automatically
lessons.2.slides.5.questions.3.explanati: Pinot Noir's thin skins contain less total tannin than thick-skinned Cabernet Sauvignon, but those tannins can become harsh and grippy if aggressively extracted. Burgundy winemakers therefore apply lighter pigeage — 1–2 times daily versus Bordeaux's 3–4 — to achieve elegant, silken structure rather than powerful grip.
lessons.2.slides.5.questions.4.question: How does a winemaker use press wine?
lessons.2.slides.5.questions.4.options.0: A. It is always discarded as too tannic to use
lessons.2.slides.5.questions.4.options.1: B. It replaces all the free-run wine as a more concentrated product
lessons.2.slides.5.questions.4.options.2: C. A percentage (typically 5–20%) is blended back into the free-run wine to add structure
lessons.2.slides.5.questions.4.options.3: D. It is sold separately as a lower-quality wine
lessons.2.slides.5.questions.4.explanati: Winemakers carefully evaluate each fraction of press wine and add the best-quality portions back to the free-run wine in calculated percentages. Too little adds no backbone; too much makes the wine harsh. The final percentage is a key stylistic decision — typically 5–20% for top Burgundy.
lessons.2.slides.6.title: Summary
lessons.2.slides.6.content: Extraction in Burgundy is an exercise in restraint. Gentle pigeage, calibrated use of remontage and careful selection of press wine fractions all serve the same goal: capturing the colour, aromatics and structure of Pinot Noir without tipping into harsh over-extraction.
lessons.3.title: Oak Aging and Élevage
lessons.3.slides.0.title: Oak Aging and Élevage
lessons.3.slides.0.subtitle: 12 minutes
lessons.3.slides.0.description: How the choice of barrel — its age, toast level and source — shapes the final character of Burgundy red wines during the critical aging period.
lessons.3.slides.1.title: 🛢️ The Burgundy Barrel (Pièce Bourguignonne)
lessons.3.slides.1.content: The standard Burgundy barrel — the pièce bourguignonne — holds 228 litres (as opposed to Bordeaux's 225-litre barrique). The small barrel size maximises the wood-to-wine ratio, allowing gentle but efficient flavour integration.
lessons.3.slides.1.keyPoints.0: Capacity: 228 litres (Burgundy pièce) vs 225 litres (Bordeaux barrique)
lessons.3.slides.1.keyPoints.1: Wood species: French oak (Quercus sessilis/petraea) — predominant; adds spice, vanilla and structure
lessons.3.slides.1.keyPoints.2: Top coopers: François Frères, Seguin Moreau, Taransaud, Rousseau
lessons.3.slides.1.keyPoints.3: Forest source: Allier, Vosges, Tronçais — each contributes different grain tightness and flavour
lessons.3.slides.2.title: 📊 New Oak Percentage and Its Effect
lessons.3.slides.2.content: The percentage of new oak barrels used is the primary lever controlling how much oak flavour enters the wine. This decision defines stylistic identity and is hotly debated in Burgundy.
lessons.3.slides.2.keyPoints.0: 100% new oak (bois neuf): maximum oak integration; richness and toasty complexity; traditional at some prestigious domaines
lessons.3.slides.2.keyPoints.1: 30–50% new oak: balanced approach for Premier Cru and Grand Cru; moderate spice without dominating fruit
lessons.3.slides.2.keyPoints.2: 0–20% new oak: modern minimal-intervention style; oak barely perceptible; pure terroir expression prioritised
lessons.3.slides.2.keyPoints.3: Trend: new generation of producers reducing new oak — 'let the fruit speak'
lessons.3.slides.3.title: ⏳ Duration of Barrel Aging
lessons.3.slides.3.content: The length of time wine spends in barrel affects oxidative development, tannin softening and flavour integration.
lessons.3.slides.3.keyPoints.0: Typical duration: 12–18 months for Village and Premier Cru; up to 18–24 months for Grand Cru
lessons.3.slides.3.keyPoints.1: Racking (soutirage): wine is transferred between barrels (2–3 times) to clarify and aerate gently
lessons.3.slides.3.keyPoints.2: Topping up (ouillage): barrels are topped weekly to replace wine lost to evaporation ('angel's share')
lessons.3.slides.3.keyPoints.3: Lees contact: some estates leave wine on fine lees in barrel for added texture and complexity (bâtonnage less common for reds)
lessons.3.slides.4.title: 💡 Key Take-aways
lessons.3.slides.4.points.0: 🍷 The pièce bourguignonne (228L) is Burgundy's standard barrel — its small size encourages gentle but efficient flavour integration
lessons.3.slides.4.points.1: 🍷 New oak percentage is the most powerful lever in Burgundy barrel aging — the trend is toward less
lessons.3.slides.4.points.2: 🍷 Grand Cru wines typically age 18–24 months; Village wines 12–15 months
lessons.3.slides.4.points.3: 🍷 French oak forests (Allier, Vosges, Tronçais) each impart subtly different characteristics
lessons.3.slides.5.title: 🧠 Knowledge Check
lessons.3.slides.5.questions.0.question: What is the capacity of a standard Burgundy barrel (pièce bourguignonne)?
lessons.3.slides.5.questions.0.explanati: The standard Burgundy barrel — the pièce bourguignonne — holds 228 litres, compared with the 225-litre barrique used in Bordeaux. The small barrel size creates a high wood-to-wine ratio, facilitating efficient flavour and tannin integration.
lessons.3.slides.5.questions.1.question: What does a higher percentage of new oak contribute to a Burgundy red wine?
lessons.3.slides.5.questions.1.options.0: A. Lower tannin and lighter body
lessons.3.slides.5.questions.1.options.1: B. Higher acidity and less colour
lessons.3.slides.5.questions.1.options.2: C. Greater oak flavour — vanilla, toast, spice — and richer texture
lessons.3.slides.5.questions.1.options.3: D. Faster reduction and lower alcohol
lessons.3.slides.5.questions.1.explanati: New oak barrels release more vanillin, toasty compounds and tannins into the wine than older, 'neutral' barrels. A high new oak percentage adds richness, vanilla and complexity — but risks overwhelming the delicate Pinot Noir fruit if used excessively. The modern trend in Burgundy is toward lower new oak percentages.
lessons.3.slides.5.questions.2.question: How long is a typical Grand Cru Burgundy aged in barrel?
lessons.3.slides.5.questions.2.explanati: Grand Cru Burgundy is typically aged in barrel for 18–24 months, allowing sufficient time for tannin softening, flavour integration and controlled oxidative development. Village wines are aged for a shorter period — usually 12–15 months — as they do not require the same extended development.
lessons.3.slides.5.questions.3.question: What is 'ouillage' (topping up) in barrel aging?
lessons.3.slides.5.questions.3.options.0: A. Adding sugar to wine to increase alcohol
lessons.3.slides.5.questions.3.options.1: B. Regularly refilling barrels with the same wine to replace liquid lost to evaporation
lessons.3.slides.5.questions.3.options.2: C. Transferring wine from one barrel to another to aerate it
lessons.3.slides.5.questions.3.options.3: D. Tasting wine from the barrel with a thief (pipette)
lessons.3.slides.5.questions.3.explanati: Ouillage is the practice of regularly topping up barrels with the same wine to replace the 'angel's share' — wine lost to evaporation through the wood. Without topping up, air would enter the headspace and oxidise the wine prematurely.
lessons.3.slides.5.questions.4.question: Which French oak forest is most associated with tight grain and subtle, refined oak character?
lessons.3.slides.5.questions.4.explanati: The Allier forest in central France is celebrated for producing tight-grained, finely textured oak that imparts subtle, refined spice and vanilla flavours. Many top Burgundy producers prefer Allier staves for their Premiers Crus and Grands Crus, alongside the similarly prized Tronçais and Vosges forests.
lessons.3.slides.6.title: Summary
lessons.3.slides.6.content: Barrel aging in Burgundy is a precisely calibrated balance between introducing complexity through wood and preserving the purity and terroir expression of the Pinot Noir fruit. The trend toward less new oak reflects growing confidence in letting the vineyard — not the cellar — speak.
